reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Results from bacterial contamination of the peritoneal cavity following perforation, ischaemia, or inflammation of an abdominal viscus, unlike primary (spontaneous) peritonitis
Presents with severe, constant abdominal pain worsened by movement, with tenderness, guarding, rigidity, and rebound, and the patient characteristically lies still
Common sources include perforated peptic ulcer, perforated appendix, perforated diverticular disease, and bowel ischaemia or anastomotic leak
Systemic features of sepsis develop rapidly: fever, tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, and, if untreated, septic shock and multi-organ failure
The management triad is aggressive resuscitation, appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics, and prompt source control of the underlying cause
Source control, achieved surgically or by radiological drainage, is the definitive step; antibiotics and resuscitation support but do not replace it
Faeculent peritonitis from colonic perforation carries a particularly heavy bacterial and endotoxin load and a high mortality
Peritoneal contamination is often graded (localised, diffuse, purulent, faeculent) and guides the extent of surgery and lavage
reference.pathophysiology: Secondary peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum caused by spillage of gastrointestinal contents and micro-organisms into the peritoneal cavity following a breach of a hollow viscus or transmural necrosis. Gut flora, typically a mix of coliforms and anaerobes, provoke an intense inflammatory response with fibrinopurulent exudate, large third-space fluid losses, and paralytic ileus. Absorption of bacteria and endotoxin across the vast peritoneal surface drives systemic inflammatory response, sepsis, and septic shock. The peritoneum may localise infection into abscesses, but diffuse contamination overwhelms these defences and threatens life.
additionalDifferentials: Medical causes of acute abdomen (diabetic ketoacidosis, inferior myocardial infarction)
additionalInvestigations: Bloods including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, CRP, amylase or lipase, blood cultures, and lactate
Arterial blood gas to assess acid-base status and organ perfusion
Erect chest radiograph for free subdiaphragmatic gas
CT abdomen and pelvis to identify the source and any collections
Peritoneal fluid sampling and culture when the diagnosis or source is unclear
redFlags: Generalised peritonitis with sepsis, hypotension, or rising lactate indicating septic shock (surgical emergency)
Faeculent contamination from colonic perforation with heavy sepsis burden
Progressive organ dysfunction (oliguria, confusion, respiratory compromise)
Failure to improve after resuscitation, indicating inadequate source control
reference.prognosis: Outcome hinges on early recognition, prompt resuscitation, and timely source control; delay, faeculent contamination, advanced age, and comorbidity markedly increase mortality, which remains high in established diffuse peritonitis with septic shock.
pitfalls: Delaying source control while awaiting response to antibiotics and fluids
Under-resuscitating a patient with large third-space and septic losses
Attributing peritonism to a medical cause and missing a surgical source
Inadequate peritoneal lavage or failing to address ongoing contamination at surgery
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
